name: The doctrine of the golden mean
plain_explanation: Every virtue, Aristotle argues, lies at a mid-point between two opposite vices -- one of excess, one of deficiency. Courage, for example, is the mean between the excess of rashness and the deficiency of cowardice.
precise_definition: The doctrine that moral virtue is a disposition to feel and act in a way that is intermediate between two vicious extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency, relative to the particular person and situation -- e.g. courage between cowardice and rashness, liberality between prodigality and meanness, proper pride between vanity and humility.
why_it_mattered: It became the most famous and influential single doctrine of Aristotle's ethics, offering a systematic method for identifying virtues by locating the extremes on either side of them.
historical_origin: Developed across Books II-IV of the Nicomachean Ethics.
examples: Courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness
Liberality as the mean between prodigality and meanness
Ready wit as the mean between buffoonery and boorishness
Truthfulness (about oneself) as the mean between boastfulness and mock-modesty
objections: Russell notes the scheme does not obviously fit truthfulness in any wider sense than truthfulness about oneself, and mocks a real-life mayor who claimed to have steered a mean between 'partiality' and 'impartiality'
It cannot apply to intellectual contemplation, which the Ethics elsewhere calls the best of all activities -- there being no vice of 'excess' of contemplation on Aristotle's own account
influence_on_later_thinkers: Became a standard reference point in virtue ethics down to the present.
